cases.line: You have backups running every night and a green tick in the dashboard to prove it. That tick means the job finished. It does not mean anything inside it can be read back.
cases.query: server rack status lights

cases.line: Backups fail quietly. A path changes, a credential expires, a disk fills, and the job still reports success because it did everything it was asked to do. The gap between finished and usable is where the outage lives.
cases.query: hands holding damaged hard drive

cases.line: Restore it. Pick a random file from last month, pull it out of the backup onto a clean machine, and open it. If that takes you longer than an hour, you do not have a backup. You have a hope.

cases.line: Put one restore in the calendar every quarter and treat a failed restore as an incident. The first one will find something broken. That is the point.

cases.line: You added a database index to make your queries run faster, but now your application feels sluggish. You thought indexes were pure upside. They are not.

cases.line: You believed that organizing your table helps the database work less overall. In reality, you gave the engine extra chores to finish before saving any data.

cases.line: The working set grows larger with every new index you create. Soon the index no longer fits in memory, forcing the server to fetch missing blocks from slow spinning disks on every write.

cases.line: Every index you delete is a heavy tax you refuse to pay twice.

cases.line: You have probably searched for flights by typing a phrase into a box and hoping the machine just gets what you mean. That loose approach works fine until a vague filter misses the one cheap ticket you actually needed, costing you hundreds of dollars on your summer vacation.
cases.query: person typing at keyboard

cases.line: Most people assume standard search bars understand grammar because they handle human sentences with surprising ease. They do not. Natural language is messy, full of hidden ambiguities, and computers cannot process poetry without breaking into total confusion.
cases.query: handwritten notes on paper

cases.line: Predicate logic fixes this gap by splitting every sentence into two distinct pieces. You have constant nouns representing concrete objects, and you have predicates acting as properties or relationships. This turns a fuzzy thought into a sharp statement about the world.
cases.query: wooden blocks on table

cases.line: When you write sloppy queries for a massive customer database, the software pulls thousands of irrelevant records because it cannot parse your loose phrasing. That mistake floods your server with garbage data, crashing the application right when traffic peaks.
cases.query: frustrated office worker

cases.line: Translate your vague requirements into strict predicate statements before you write a single line of code. Define your constants clearly, bind your variables with the right quantifiers, and test every logical branch against edge cases.
cases.query: whiteboard with flowcharts

cases.line: Master the predicate, and you will finally speak the native tongue of computation.
